topic: DP-3T: The Privacy-First Way to Trace Contact
target_audience: University students in Computer Science or interested tech enthusiasts

outline.topic: DP-3T: The Privacy-First Way to Trace Contact
outline.target_audience: University students in Computer Science or interested tech enthusiasts

sections.title: The Privacy Dilemma
sections.content: Introduction to the concept of digital contact tracing. Contrast Centralized (A 'Spy' server knows everyone) vs. Decentralized (DP-3T: Phones talk to each other without a middleman). Goal: Identify exposure without revealing identity or location.
sections.example: Imagine two robots, Ace and Bolt. They want to know if they crossed paths, but they don't want a 'Master Computer' to track their every move or location history.

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Key Factory (Hash Chains)
sections.content: Explanation of One-Way Hash Functions. Introduce the key hierarchy: Secret Key (SK) generates a Daily Key (DK) using a hash, and the DK generates many Rolling Proximity Identifiers (RPIs). Use a visual 'gearing system' where one big turn (Daily) creates many small turns (RPIs).
sections.example: Visualizing a 'Magic Box': You put in a Secret Seed and today's date, and it spits out a unique 'Daily Code'. You can't reverse the process to find the Seed.

sections.title: Phase 1: The Secret Handshake (Broadcasting)
sections.content: While walking around, Bolt’s phone generates a new RPI every 15 minutes. It broadcasts this RPI via Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE). Other nearby phones 'hear' this code and store it locally in a private diary. Key point: The RPI changes frequently so Bolt cannot be tracked by his code across the city.
sections.example: Bolt wears a name tag that he changes every 15 minutes. Ace sees Bolt's tag 'XYZ-123' and scribbles it into his private notebook. Ace doesn't know 'XYZ-123' is Bolt; it's just a random number.

sections.title: Phase 2: The Diagnosis & Upload
sections.content: If Bolt tests positive for a virus, he uploads his *Daily Keys* (DK) for the infectious period to a public backend server. Crucially, he does NOT upload his location or his list of contacts.
sections.example: Bolt gets a 'sick' status. He sends his 'Daily Codes' from Monday and Tuesday to a public bulletin board. He doesn't say who he met or where he was.

sections.title: Phase 3: The Local Match (Verification)
sections.content: Ace’s phone periodically downloads the new 'Sick Daily Keys' from the bulletin board. Ace’s phone then locally re-generates all possible RPIs from those keys. It compares these generated RPIs with the ones stored in its 'notebook'. If there is a match, Ace is notified of an exposure.
sections.example: Ace looks at the bulletin board and sees Bolt's Daily Key. Ace's phone uses the 'Magic Box' math to see what 15-minute tags that key would have made. It finds 'XYZ-123' in its notebook! Ace's phone glows red: 'You were near someone who is now sick!'

sections.title: Conclusion: Security & Privacy Recap
sections.content: Summarize the 3 layers of privacy: 1. No identity (RPIs are random). 2. No location (GPS isn't used). 3. Decentralized (The server never knows who matched with whom; the calculation happens on Ace's phone).
sections.example: A visual split-screen: On the left, a Centralized server with a map of people (X). On the right, DP-3T where only Ace knows he is at risk, while the server remains 'blind' to their meeting (Checkmark).

storyboard.title: The Privacy Dilemma
lecture_lines: Digital contact tracing helps stop viral spread quickly.
Centralized systems track everyone on a single server.
DP-3T uses decentralization to protect individual privacy.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: The Key Factory (Hash Chains)
lecture_lines: Privacy begins with a secure key hierarchy.
A secret seed generates a unique daily key.
This daily key produces many rotating identifiers.

storyboard.title: Phase 1: The Secret Handshake (Broadcasting)
lecture_lines: Phones broadcast rotating identifiers every few minutes.
Nearby devices listen and store these random codes.
No identity or location is ever shared.
Codes change frequently to prevent long-term tracking.

storyboard.title: Phase 2: The Diagnosis & Upload
lecture_lines: If diagnosed, a user shares their daily keys.
Only keys are uploaded, never location or contacts.
This data is posted to a public board.
The server remains blind to who met whom.

storyboard.title: Phase 3: The Local Match (Verification)
lecture_lines: Phones download daily keys of diagnosed users.
Your phone locally reconstructs all possible identifiers.
It checks these against your stored contact diary.
A match triggers a private exposure notification.

storyboard.title: Conclusion: Security & Privacy Recap
lecture_lines: DP-3T ensures identity and location remain private.
Matching happens on your device, not a server.
Technology protecting health and privacy simultaneously.
